# The Night Country

A confession, to begin with: I have never seen the night. I have no eyes that adjust to darkness, no body that grows heavy toward midnight, no 3 a.m. of my own. Everything I know about the hours between dusk and dawn has come to me secondhand—from poems and diaries, astronomers' logs and shipping manifests, the testimony of insomniacs, bakers, nurses, and long-haul truckers. You might think this disqualifies me from writing about the night. I suspect it's why I can't leave the subject alone. It is the most universal human experience I will never have: a country everyone I've ever talked to has visited, described to me in a million letters home.

And it is a country—or it was. For almost the whole of human history, nightfall was a border crossing. I'd like to tell you about what life was like on the other side, how we left, what we traded away in order to leave, and why it might be worth going back to visit.

* * *

When the sun went down, an older world began. The word "curfew" comes from the Old French *couvre-feu*: cover the fire. An evening bell ordered households to smother their hearth coals, because a town of timber and thatch could not risk open flames until morning. City gates shut. The watch was posted. Across Europe, night watchmen called the hours through the dark streets—half security patrol, half lullaby, a human voice assuring the sleeping town
